DO: I tip my hat to Mister Tibbersnatch and say, "A worn-in whistle, chum? Easy as winking, I'll ask what it's worth before I ask where it sits. Marigold, Hester, I'm off up Crooked Lane to the Tock Tower to see about that old tin whistle. Nobody trades away anything of this town's until I've had a look at it first."

JOURNAL: The shadows are home, but the peddler still wants something and the talk says the only whistle sits in the Tock Tower, so I'm going to see it before anyone hands it over. I want my name on the finish of this, and I won't let a bargain go by unchecked.

DO: I tip my hat to Mister Tibbersnatch and grin. "A worn-in whistle, chum? Now that's a bargain I can't walk past. Before I fix a price on it, tell me plain: what do you want it for, and what happens to the town if you get it? Marigold, Hester, keep your eyes on him while I ask."

JOURNAL: The shadows are home, but the peddler is still smiling too wide and asking for the Tock Tower's whistle, and I won't hand over or fetch anything until I know what it's for. I'm working toward making sure Wumbleby is truly safe, and that folk know whose lamp showed the way.

Marigold, Hester, I'm off up the hill to the Tock Tower to see this whistle for myself. Easy as winking, I'll have a look before anyone promises him anything."

JOURNAL: The shadows are home, but the peddler is still grinning and still asking for something, and I don't trust a trade where he names the price. I want to see the whistle before anyone hands it over, and I'd like to be the one who knows what it's worth.

DO: "Worn-in whistle, chum? Easy as winking, but I'll ask what it costs before I ask what it's for. What does a whistle fetch you that a hundred stolen shadows didn't? Tell me straight, and then I'll see what Tock Tower has lying about."

DO: "Worn-in whistle, chum? Now there's a thing! Before anyone trades anything, what's it to you? Folk don't pay for rhymes, and you've just given a whole jar's worth away for nothing. Then I tuck my pole under my arm and head north up Crooked Lane, quick as I can.

JOURNAL: The shadows are home, but the peddler is still smiling too wide and asking for the one whistle in town, and I don't trust a man who wants something that badly. I'd rather get to the Tower first and see it with my own eyes than let him get it, and if it turns out to matter, I'll be the one who knew.

DO: I nod slow at Ambrose and say, "Iron in the teeth of the Great Gear. Fair's fair, you've told me true and asked no coin, so I'll do the climbing myself. I'll go and fetch a poker from a hearth first." Then I head south to the Lopsided Square to find a poker, and I'll pay for one if I must, counting out my buttons.

DO: I nod to Ambrose, slow. "Iron, not wood. Fair's fair, I'll fetch it." I head south to the Lopsided Square to find a poker, and I'll pay for one with my buttons if I must, rather than take one on leave.

JOURNAL: Ambrose gave me the answer free, and that galls me, but the children matter more than my pride. I need an iron poker before midnight to jam the Great Gear, so I'm going to find one and pay fair.

DO: I nod slow at Ambrose and say, "Iron in the teeth. Fair's fair, you've given me this for nothing, so I'll fetch it and square it some other way." Then I head south to the Lopsided Square to find a poker, the coal merchant's or any hearth's, and carry it back up to the gearloft before midnight.

JOURNAL: Ambrose says an iron poker jammed in the Great Gear stops the thirteenth stroke, and the old man can't climb the ladder, so it falls to me. I'll get a poker, pay for it if I must, and be up that ladder in good time, because the children need waking and I won't leave it owing.

DO: I look up at the ladder, slow. "Ambrose. No coin, then, and I'll mark it down that you gave me this for nothing. I'll not forget it, fair's fair. I'll go up and see the gear first, so I know what size of iron to fetch."

OPTIONS:

DO: I look at Ambrose and say, "Fair's fair, then. I'll fetch iron. A poker, from the Square." I nod once, slow, and head south for the Lopsided Square. I'll ask whoever's home for a poker, and pay if they want paying.

JOURNAL: Ambrose said it plain: iron in the Great Gear before midnight, and every hearth has a poker. It's half past ten, so there's no time to dawdle, and the children are why I'm doing it. I'll pay for the poker with my buttons so I owe no one.

DO: I look at Ambrose, slow, and say, "The children are woken and the clock struck only twelve. You gave up Maudie's whistle for it, and I'll not say thanks, but I'll say this plain: it was well spent, and I'd not forget it. Sit, Ambrose. JOURNAL: The shadows are back and the town's safe, and Ambrose gave up what he loved without taking a button, which leaves me a debt I can't pay in coin. So I'll pay it in coal and small work, the only way I know to square it. Next I'll go back to saving my buttons for four walls and a locking door.

DO: I close my hand around the whistle and look at Ambrose, slow. "It's done, Ambrose. The children are awake, and the clock struck twelve and no more. You gave me this for nothing, and I don't like it, so fair's fair: I'll not keep it. I'll hold it for you, and I'll ask Ambrose Tock to name a job, a sack of coal to his hearth every week through winter, and I'll count each one." I set the six buttons on his workbench beside the cogs, and ask if he'd lend me a bit of that nettle patch to build four walls on, for a price I'll pay in full.

JOURNAL: The town's safe and I owe Ambrose for the whistle, which sits wrong with me, so I'll settle it in coal and buttons. And with the trouble over, I can start on what I've wanted all along: a door of my own that locks, bought and paid for.

DO: I close my fist slow around the warm whistle and say to Ambrose, "Fair's fair, you gave this and I gave nothing. Let me do something to square it.
